t.1.68.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When Duḥṣanta had made his promise and departed, the fair-thighed Śakuntalā brought forth her child, a boy of boundless might.
t.1.68.3: Then Kaṇva, the best of those who perform meritorious deeds, had the sacraments beginning with the birth rite performed for that wise and growing boy.
t.1.68.4: With white, pointed teeth, built like a lion, youthful, his hands marked with the sign of the discus, glorious, large-headed and of great strength, the boy, resembling a child of the gods, quickly grew up there.
t.1.68.2: When three full years had passed, O Janamejaya, she brought forth Dauḥṣanti, whose radiance equalled that of a blazing fire, and who was endowed with beauty, nobility and fine qualities.
t.1.68.7: Then those who dwelt in Kaṇva's hermitage gave him a name: "Let this one be Sarvadamana, for he subdues everything."
t.1.68.6: Having bound them to the trees all around the hermitage, the mighty boy runs about, mounting them, taming them, and playing with them.
t.1.68.5: While still a boy of only six years, he, around the hermitage of Kaṇva, took tigers, lions and boars, elephants and buffaloes as well…
t.1.68.8: That boy, Sarvadamana by name, came to be endowed with valor, with vigor, and with strength.
t.1.68.9: Seeing that boy and his superhuman deeds, the seer said to Śakuntalā, "The time has come for his consecration as heir apparent."
t.1.68.10: Perceiving that strength of his, Kaṇva said to his disciples: "Quickly conduct this Śakuntalā, together with her son, from this hermitage to her husband this very day, she who is honored for all her auspicious marks."
t.1.68.12: Saying "So be it," all those men of boundless energy set out for Gajasāhvaya, placing Śakuntalā and her son at their head.
t.1.68.11: For a long stay of women among their kinsfolk is not approved, as it destroys their good name, their conduct and their dharma; therefore lead her away without delay.
t.1.68.13: Then the radiant woman, taking her lotus-eyed son, who shone like the offspring of an immortal, came from the forest known to Duḥṣanta.
t.1.68.14: Having approached the king, and her arrival having been made known, she was led in, together with that very son of hers, whose splendor was like that of the newly risen sun.
t.1.68.15: Having honored him as was proper, Śakuntalā said to him: "O king, let this son be consecrated by you to the office of heir apparent."
t.1.68.16: For this son, O king, godlike, was begotten by you in me; act toward him in accordance with our agreement, O best of men.
t.1.68.18: Then the king, as soon as he heard her words, though he remembered, said, "I do not remember. Whose are you, wicked ascetic woman?"
t.1.68.17: Remember, O illustrious one, the agreement that you made before, at our union in Kaṇva's hermitage.
t.1.68.19: I do not remember any bond of dharma, kāma, or artha with you. Go or stay as you please, or do whatever else you wish.
t.1.68.20: Thus addressed, the proud woman with lovely hips stood as if ashamed, and as if senseless with grief, motionless like a post.
t.1.68.21: Her eyes copper-red with fury and indignation, her pressed lips trembling, she looked askance at the king, as if burning him with her sidelong glances.
t.1.68.23: She, filled with grief and indignation, reflected for what seemed but a moment; then, gazing intently at her husband, she spoke these words in anger.
t.1.68.22: Hiding her outward expression, though stirred by anger, she then held in check the fiery energy she had amassed through austerity.
t.1.68.24: Though you know, great king, why do you speak thus, saying without scruple, “I do not know,” just as some other common man would?
t.1.68.26: He who, being one thing, presents himself as another, what sin has not been committed by that thief, the stealer of his own self?
t.1.68.27: You think, "I am alone," but you do not know the ancient sage who dwells in the heart; it is in his very presence, he who knows every wicked deed, that you commit this wrong.
t.1.68.25: In this matter I know your heart, in both its truth and its falsehood. Alas, noble one, you yourself are the witness; do not hold yourself in contempt.
t.1.68.28: Having done an evil deed, one thinks, "No one knows me." But the gods know him, and so does his own inner Person.
t.1.68.29: The sun and the moon, the wind and the fire, the sky, the earth, the waters, the heart, and Yama, the day and the night, both twilights, and Dharma know the conduct of a man.
t.1.68.30: Yama Vaivasvata wipes away the evil deeds of the man with whom the Knower of the Field, the witness of his acts who dwells in his heart, is pleased.
t.1.68.31: But the evil-souled man with whom he is not pleased, that doer of wicked deeds Yama makes pay for his misdeed.
t.1.68.33: Do not despise me, a devoted wife, thinking, "She has come of her own accord." You do not honor me, your wife, who deserves the guest-offering and has come to you of her own will.
t.1.68.34: Why do you disregard me in the assembly as if I were some common woman? Surely I am not crying out this into an empty wilderness; why do you not listen to me?
t.1.68.32: Despising himself by his own self, he passes himself off as other than he is; the gods do not bring good to one for whom not even his own self is the measure of truth.
t.1.68.35: If you will not do what I say, though I am entreating you, Duḥṣanta, then your head will burst into a hundred pieces today.
t.1.68.36: Because the husband, having entered his wife, is himself born again from her, the ancient poets know this to be the wifehood of a jāyā, she in whom one is born.
t.1.68.38: Because a son rescues his father from the hell called Put, he was therefore called putra by the Self-Existent One himself.
t.1.68.39: She is a wife who is skilled in the household; she is a wife who bears children; she is a wife whose very life is her husband; she is a wife who is devoted to her husband.
t.1.68.37: The offspring that is born of a man versed in sacred tradition, by continuing the line, delivers his forefathers who have departed before.
t.1.68.41: Those who have wives can perform the sacred rites; those with wives are true householders. Those who have wives rejoice, and those who have wives are endowed with prosperity.
t.1.68.40: The wife is half of a man; the wife is his very best friend. The wife is the root of the three aims of life; the wife is the friend of one who is about to die.
t.1.68.42: These sweet-spoken women are friends in solitude, fathers in the duties of dharma, and mothers to one who is in distress.
t.1.68.43: Even in the wilderness there is rest for a man who travels the road; he who has his wife with him is to be trusted, and therefore wives are the highest refuge.
t.1.68.45: A wife who has died first goes on beyond and waits for her husband; and if the husband has died first, the virtuous wife follows him afterward.
t.1.68.44: Even when the husband has died and wanders through the cycle of rebirth, falling alone into perilous places, it is the wife alone who follows him, she who is ever devoted to her husband.
t.1.68.47: The wise say that the self, begotten by the self itself, is called a son. Therefore a man should look upon his wife, the mother of his son, as he would his own mother.
t.1.68.46: For this reason, O king, the taking of the hand in marriage is desired, so that the husband may obtain his wife both in this world and in the next.
t.1.68.48: Beholding the son begotten on his wife, like his own face in a mirror, the father rejoices, as a doer of good deeds rejoices on reaching heaven.
t.1.68.49: Men burning with sorrows of the mind and afflicted by diseases find delight in their own wives, as those oppressed by heat find delight in waters.
t.1.68.50: Even when deeply angered, a wise man should not say anything unkind to women, seeing that pleasure, joy, and dharma all depend upon them.
t.1.68.51: Women are the eternal, holy field of one's own birth. What power have even the seers to create offspring without a woman?
t.1.68.52: When a son, running up covered with the dust of the earth, embraces his father's limbs, what could be greater than that?
t.1.68.53: This son of yours has come to you of his own accord, full of longing, and gazes at you with a sidelong glance; why then do you, such as you are, disdain him?
t.1.68.54: Ants carry their own eggs and do not break them; how then could you, knowing what dharma is, not support your own son?
t.1.68.55: Neither the touch of garments, nor of beautiful women, nor of waters is as pleasant as the touch of one's own infant son being embraced.
t.1.68.56: The brāhmaṇa is the best of two-footed beings, the cow the most excellent of four-footed ones; the guru is the foremost of the venerable, and a son is the best of all things to be touched.
t.1.68.57: Let this son of yours, so lovely to behold, embrace you and touch you; for in this world there is no touch more pleasant than the touch of a son.
t.1.68.58: When three years had passed, O tamer of foes, I gave birth to this boy, O king of kings, who will banish your sorrow.
t.1.68.59: "The Paurava shall be the performer of a hundred horse sacrifices": thus a voice in the sky addressed me long ago, at the time of his birth.
t.1.68.61: The twice-born recite this sacred formula from the Vedas as well, at the birth ceremony of sons; and you too know it to be so.
t.1.68.60: Surely men who have gone off to another village lovingly lift their sons onto their laps, kiss them on the head, and greet them with joy.
t.1.68.62: From limb after limb you come into being; from the heart you are born. You are indeed one's own self, bearing the name of son; so live a hundred autumns.
t.1.68.64: Born from your own limbs, this is another man sprung from a man; behold my son as a second self of yours, as if reflected in a clear lake.
t.1.68.65: For just as the āhavanīya fire is led forth from the gārhapatya fire, so this one is born from you; you, though being one, have been made twofold.
t.1.68.63: For my sustenance depends on you, and so does my imperishable lineage; therefore, my child, live in great happiness for a hundred autumns.
t.1.68.67: Urvaśī and Pūrvacitti, Sahajanyā and Menakā, Viśvācī and Ghṛtācī: these six alone are the foremost of the Apsarases.
t.1.68.66: For, O king, while you were roaming about on the hunt, drawn away by a deer, I, a maiden, was approached by you in my father's hermitage.
t.1.68.70: What evil deed, I wonder, have I done in a former birth, that I was abandoned by my kinsfolk in childhood and now by you as well?
t.1.68.68: Among them, the excellent apsaras named Menakā, sprung from Brahman, came down from the heavens to the earth and bore me by Viśvāmitra.
t.1.68.72: Duḥṣanta said: I do not recognize any son born of you, Śakuntalā. Women are speakers of untruth; who will believe your word?
t.1.68.71: Very well, abandoned by you, I shall go to the hermitage; but you ought not to abandon this boy, your own son, born of your very self.
t.1.68.73: Your mother is Menakā, a pitiless wanton, who cast you away on the slope of Himavant like a faded garland already offered and discarded.
t.1.68.74: And your father too, Viśvāmitra, pitiless and born of a kṣatriya womb, was greedy for brahminhood and wholly given over to lust.
t.1.68.76: Are you not ashamed to speak these incredible words, especially in my presence? Wicked ascetic woman, be gone!
t.1.68.75: Menakā is the foremost of the Apsarases, and your father the foremost of the great seers; why then would you, their offspring, speak like a wanton woman?
t.1.68.77: Where is the great seer, ever fierce, and where is that Apsaras Menakā? And where are you, so wretched, wearing the garb of a female ascetic?
t.1.68.78: And this son of yours is huge of body and strong, though only a boy; how in so short a time has he shot up like the trunk of a śāla tree?
t.1.68.69: That apsaras Menakā gave birth to me on the slope of Himavant, and, casting me away, she departed, like a wicked woman abandoning the child of another.
t.1.68.79: Your origin is very low, and you appear to me a wanton woman; for you were born of Menakā by mere chance, out of lust and passion.
t.1.68.80: All this that you are saying, O ascetic woman, is beyond my knowledge. I do not recognize you; go wherever you please.
